root_theorem.statement_nl: Suppose that each point in the plane is colored either red or green, subject to the following condition: For every three noncollinear points $A,B,C$ of the same color, the center of the circle passing through $A,B$ and $C$ is also this color. Prove that all points of the plane are the same color.

domain_restrictions: f is a total function from the Euclidean plane R^2 to the two-element set {red,green}
A,B,C,P,O are points of the Euclidean plane R^2
the hypothesis applies only to triples A,B,C that are noncollinear (hence distinct) so the circumcenter is uniquely defined in R^2
the circumcenter operation circ(A,B,C) is the unique intersection of perpendicular bisectors of AB and AC (uses Euclidean geometry)
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every function f: R^2 -> {red,green}, if for all points A,B,C in R^2 that are noncollinear and satisfy f(A)=f(B)=f(C) we have f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A), then there exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c. Equivalently: ∀f [(∀A,B,C (noncollinear ∧ f(A)=f(B)=f(C) ⇒ f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A))) ⇒ (∃c ∈ {red,green} ∀P f(P)=c)].
quantifier_order: forall f : R^2 -> {red,green} (consider any 2-coloring of the plane)
assume (hypothesis) forall A,B,C in R^2: if A,B,C are noncollinear and f(A)=f(B)=f(C) then f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A)
conclude: exists c in {red,green} such that forall P in R^2, f(P) = c

variables.name: f
variables.role: coloring function f: R^2 -> {red,green}; assigns to each plane point one of the two colors

variables.name: A
variables.role: one of three points used in the hypothesis; when quantified in hypothesis must be distinct from B,C and noncollinear with them

variables.name: O
variables.role: the circumcenter of A,B,C (well-defined only when A,B,C are noncollinear); O is computed from A,B,C

variables.name: P
variables.role: arbitrary point of the plane appearing in the conclusion 'all points of the plane are the same color'

witness_dependencies: O (the circumcenter) is an explicit function of the triple (A,B,C); i.e. O = circumcenter(A,B,C)
the existential 'there exists a monochromatic color c' depends only on the coloring function f (i.e. c = f(P0) for some chosen point P0), not on particular triples A,B,C
no existential point witness is allowed to depend on future universal choices beyond those already in the hypothesis (hypothesis quantifiers over A,B,C are universal)

selected_decomposition.strategy_summary: Use a local contradiction centered at two opposite-colored points together with an explicit finite two-circle configuration. This differs from the failed attempts by completely avoiding the false global classification of circumcenter-closed subsets, and it explicitly fixes the missing-coverage issue by using a color-transfer lemma whose hypotheses exactly match the auxiliary geometry produced by the configuration lemma.

steps.derives: Fix an arbitrary coloring f : R^2 -> {red,green} satisfying the hypothesis that for every noncollinear triple A,B,C, if f(A)=f(B)=f(C), then f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A).
steps.trivial_justification: This is the universal hypothesis of the root theorem, specialized to an arbitrary coloring f.

steps.derives: Choose an arbitrary point O in R^2 and define c := f(O). It is enough to prove that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: If every point has the same color as the chosen point O, then the coloring is constant with witness color c.

steps.derives: Assume for contradiction that there exists a point G in R^2 such that f(G) != c.
steps.trivial_justification: This is the standard contradiction setup for proving the universal statement from A2.

steps.derives: The points O and G are distinct, because equal points have equal colors. Therefore r := dist(O,G) is a positive real number.
steps.trivial_justification: From A2, f(O)=c. From A3, f(G)≠c. Hence O≠G. Euclidean distance between distinct points is positive, so dist(O,G)>0.

steps.derives: Define s := r/4. Then 0 < s < r/2.
steps.trivial_justification: Since r>0 by A4, dividing by 4 gives s>0. Also r/4<r/2 for positive r.

steps.derives: There exist five pairwise distinct points X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4,X_5 on Circle(G,s) and, for each i in {1,2,3,4,5}, points A_i,B_i on Circle(O,r) such that all ten support points A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5 are pairwise distinct and each X_i is the circumcenter of the noncollinear triangle O A_i B_i.
steps.trivial_justification: Apply L3 to the distinct points O,G and the real number s with 0<s<r/2 established in A5.

steps.derives: Among the ten support points A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5 on Circle(O,r), at most two have color different from c.
steps.trivial_justification: By A2, c=f(O). By A6, every support point lies on Circle(O,r). Lemma L1, applied to f, O, and r, says that Circle(O,r) contains at most two points whose color differs from f(O)=c. Therefore at most two of the ten support points are not color c.

steps.derives: There exist at least three distinct indices i in {1,2,3,4,5} such that both A_i and B_i have color c.
steps.trivial_justification: The ten support points are pairwise distinct by A6, and A7 says that at most two of them are not color c. Lemma L4 then implies that among the five labeled pairs (A_i,B_i), at least three pairs are entirely color c.

steps.derives: For each index i found in A8, the point X_i has color c. Hence there exist three distinct points among X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4,X_5 lying on Circle(G,s) and colored c.
steps.trivial_justification: Fix any index i supplied by A8. Then f(A_i)=f(B_i)=c, and A2 gives f(O)=c. Step A6 states that O,A_i,B_i are noncollinear and that X_i is the circumcenter of triangle O A_i B_i. Applying L2 yields f(X_i)=c. Doing this for the three indices from A8 gives three c-colored auxiliary points. They are distinct because the X_i are pairwise distinct in A6, and they lie on Circle(G,s) by A6.
By A9, there are three distinct points on Circle(G,s) all colored c. Since s>0 by A5, Lemma L5 applies and shows that the center G also has color c.

steps.derives: This contradicts the assumption that f(G) != c. Therefore every point P in R^2 satisfies f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: A3 assumed the existence of a point G with color different from c, while A10 proves that this same point G has color c. Hence no such G can exist. Therefore all points have color c.

steps.derives: There exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: Take the witness c=f(O) from A2. Step A11 proves that every point has color c.

steps.derives: For every function f: R^2 -> {red,green}, if for all points A,B,C in R^2 that are noncollinear and satisfy f(A)=f(B)=f(C) we have f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A), then there exists a color c in {red,green} such that for every point P in R^2, f(P)=c.
steps.trivial_justification: A1 fixed an arbitrary coloring f under the stated hypothesis, and A12 established exactly the desired conclusion for that arbitrary f.

assembly_plan.proof_skeleton_nl: Fix an arbitrary coloring f satisfying the monochromatic-circumcenter property. Choose any point O and call its color c. To prove the coloring is constant, it suffices to show that every point has color c. Assume for contradiction that some point G has the opposite color. Let r = dist(O,G) and s = r/4, so 0 < s < r/2. Use the finite configuration lemma to choose five distinct auxiliary points X_i on the small circle centered at G of radius s, together with support pairs A_i,B_i on the large circle centered at O of radius r, in such a way that each X_i is the circumcenter of the noncollinear triangle O A_i B_i and all ten support points are pairwise distinct. Because O has color c, the large-circle bound shows that among those ten support points at most two are not color c. The combinatorial lemma then yields at least three indices i for which both A_i and B_i have color c. For each such i, the color-transfer lemma applies to triangle O A_i B_i and gives f(X_i)=c. Thus the small circle centered at G contains three distinct points of color c. Applying the circle-center lemma to that small circle forces G itself to have color c, contradicting the assumption that G had the opposite color. Therefore no opposite-colored point exists, so every point of the plane has color c. Since f was arbitrary, this proves the theorem.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let f : R^2 -> {red,green} be a coloring with the following property: for every noncollinear triple A,B,C in R^2, if f(A)=f(B)=f(C), then f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A). Fix a point O in R^2 and a real number r>0. Then the circle Circle(O,r) contains at most two points whose color is different from f(O). Equivalently, there do not exist three distinct points A,B,C on Circle(O,r) with f(A)=f(B)=f(C) != f(O).

domain_restrictions: f is a function from R^2 to the two-element set {red,green}
P(f) quantifies only over noncollinear triples (circumcenter is only asserted/used for noncollinear triples)
O is any point in R^2 and r is any strictly positive real number
In the conclusion A,B,C (if existentially asserted) are required to be distinct and lie on Circle(O,r)
Circumcenter(A,B,C) is meaningful only for noncollinear A,B,C
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every function f: R^2 -> {red,green} satisfying P(f) (where P(f) := for all noncollinear A,B,C in R^2, if f(A)=f(B)=f(C) then f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A)), for every O in R^2 and every r>0 it holds that there do not exist three distinct points A,B,C in Circle(O,r) with f(A)=f(B)=f(C) and f(A) != f(O). Equivalently: for every such f,O,r, the set {X in Circle(O,r) : f(X) != f(O)} has cardinality at most 2.
quantifier_order: forall f: (R^2 -> {red,green}) such that P(f) holds
where P(f) is: forall noncollinear A,B,C in R^2, (f(A)=f(B)=f(C) implies f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A))
forall O in R^2
forall r in R with r>0
conclusion: not (exists distinct A,B,C in Circle(O,r) with f(A)=f(B)=f(C) and f(A) != f(O))

variables.role: coloring function f: R^2 -> {red,green} (global hypothesis variable)

variables.name: Circle(O,r)

witness_dependencies: The (negated) existential in the conclusion, if it were to hold, would provide A,B,C that depend on f, O, r; i.e. any witness triple (A,B,C) would be a function of (f,O,r)
There is no global existential witness in the statement as given; the final claim is a universal-negative (¬∃) for each fixed f,O,r

lemmas.proof_nl: Assume for contradiction that Circle(O,r) contains three distinct points A, B, C whose color is different from f(O). Since f takes values only in {red,green}, all three of A, B, C must then have the same color, namely the color opposite to f(O). Thus f(A)=f(B)=f(C) and f(A) != f(O). We first show that A, B, C are noncollinear. Indeed, let l be any line, and let D be the foot of the perpendicular from O to l. For any point X on l, the right triangle ODX gives OX^2 = OD^2 + DX^2. Hence the condition X in Circle(O,r), i.e. OX = r, is equivalent to DX^2 = r^2 - OD^2, which has at most two solutions on the line l. So a line meets Circle(O,r) in at most two points. Therefore three distinct points on Circle(O,r) cannot be collinear, and A, B, C are noncollinear. Next, because OA=OB=r, the point O is equidistant from A and B, so O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AB. Likewise, OA=OC=r, so O lies on the perpendicular bisector of AC. Since A, B, C are noncollinear, their circumcenter is, by definition, the unique intersection point of these two perpendicular bisectors. Therefore circumcenter(A,B,C)=O. Now apply the hypothesis of the lemma to the noncollinear monochromatic triple A, B, C. We get f(circumcenter(A,B,C)) = f(A). Since circumcenter(A,B,C)=O, this says f(O)=f(A), contradicting f(A) != f(O). This contradiction shows that Circle(O,r) cannot contain three distinct points whose color is different from f(O). Hence it contains at most two such points. In particular, there do not exist three distinct points A, B, C on Circle(O,r) with f(A)=f(B)=f(C) != f(O).
lemmas.role_in_parent: Provides the bound that on the large circle centered at O, among the ten support points at most two can have the opposite color.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let f : R^2 -> {red,green} be a coloring with the following property: for every noncollinear triple U,V,W in R^2, if f(U)=f(V)=f(W), then f(circumcenter(U,V,W))=f(U). Let O,A,B,X be points of R^2 such that O,A,B are noncollinear and X = circumcenter(O,A,B). If f(O)=f(A)=f(B), then f(X)=f(O).

domain_restrictions: f is a total function from R^2 to the two-element set {red,green}
circumcenter(U,V,W) is only defined/meaningful when U,V,W are noncollinear
the universal property P quantifies over triples (U,V,W) restricted to noncollinear triples
O,A,B in the instance are required to be noncollinear so that X := circumcenter(O,A,B) is defined
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For every function f: R^2 -> {red,green}, assume P(f): for all U,V,W in R^2, if noncollinear(U,V,W) and f(U)=f(V)=f(W) then f(circumcenter(U,V,W)) = f(U). Then for all O,A,B in R^2, if noncollinear(O,A,B) and X := circumcenter(O,A,B), we have: if f(O)=f(A)=f(B) then f(X)=f(O).
quantifier_order: for all f : R^2 -> {red,green} such that P(f) holds (see property below)
where P(f) := for all U,V,W in R^2, if noncollinear(U,V,W) and f(U)=f(V)=f(W) then f(circumcenter(U,V,W)) = f(U)
for all O,A,B in R^2 with noncollinear(O,A,B)
let X := circumcenter(O,A,B)
then: if f(O)=f(A)=f(B) then f(X)=f(O)

in the general property, circumcenter(U,V,W) is a deterministic function of U,V,W (no additional hidden existential dependence)

lemmas.proof_nl:
Assume the hypotheses of the lemma. Thus f has the property that for all points U,V,W in R^2, if U,V,W are noncollinear and f(U)=f(V)=f(W), then f(circumcenter(U,V,W))=f(U).

Now apply this property to the specific triple U=O, V=A, W=B. By hypothesis, O,A,B are noncollinear, and also f(O)=f(A)=f(B). Therefore the assumed property yields

f(circumcenter(O,A,B)) = f(O).

But X = circumcenter(O,A,B) by hypothesis. Substituting this equality into the previous conclusion gives

f(X) = f(O).

This is exactly the desired conclusion.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Transfers the color c from O and a support pair A_i,B_i to the auxiliary point X_i once X_i is known to be the circumcenter of triangle O A_i B_i.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let O,G be distinct points of R^2, let r := dist(O,G), and let s be a real number with 0 < s < r/2. Then there exist five pairwise distinct points X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4,X_5 on Circle(G,s) and, for each index i in {1,2,3,4,5}, points A_i,B_i on Circle(O,r) such that: (i) all ten points A_1,B_1,A_2,B_2,A_3,B_3,A_4,B_4,A_5,B_5 are pairwise distinct; (ii) for each i, the points O,A_i,B_i are noncollinear; and (iii) for each i, X_i = circumcenter(O,A_i,B_i).

domain_restrictions: O,G are points in R^2 and O ≠ G
r is defined as dist(O,G) and therefore r > 0
s is a real number satisfying 0 < s < r/2
Circle(G,s) = {p ∈ R^2 : dist(p,G) = s} (hence s > 0 implies infinitely many points)
Circle(O,r) = {p ∈ R^2 : dist(p,O) = r} (r > 0)
X_i ∈ Circle(G,s) for i = 1..5 and X_i are pairwise distinct
For each i, A_i,B_i ∈ Circle(O,r)
(i) the ten points {A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5} are pairwise distinct
(ii) for each i, O,A_i,B_i are noncollinear (this is required to make circumcenter(O,A_i,B_i) well-defined as the unique circumcenter of a noncollinear triple)
(iii) for each i, X_i = circumcenter(O,A_i,B_i)
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For all O,G ∈ R^2 with O ≠ G, let r := dist(O,G). For all real s with 0 < s < r/2, there exist points X_1,...,X_5 ∈ R^2 such that (a) for each i in {1,..,5}, dist(X_i,G) = s, (b) X_1,...,X_5 are pairwise distinct, and there exist points A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5 ∈ R^2 with each A_i,B_i satisfying dist(A_i,O)=dist(B_i,O)=r, such that (i) the ten points A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5 are pairwise distinct, (ii) for each i, the triple (O,A_i,B_i) is noncollinear, and (iii) for each i, X_i is the circumcenter of the noncollinear triple (O,A_i,B_i).
quantifier_order: forall O,G in R^2 with O ≠ G
let r := dist(O,G) (hence r > 0)
forall real s with 0 < s < r/2
exists points X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4,X_5 ∈ Circle(G,s) that are pairwise distinct
for each i in {1,2,3,4,5} exists points A_i,B_i ∈ Circle(O,r) (simultaneously) such that conditions (i)-(iii) hold

witness_dependencies: The existential tuple (X_1,...,X_5) may be chosen depending on the given O,G,s (i.e. on r and s) but not on any A_i,B_i (they are chosen later in the scope).
For each index i, the points A_i,B_i are existentially chosen after X_1,...,X_5 are fixed, so each A_i,B_i may depend on O,G,s and on the entire chosen tuple (X_1,...,X_5) and on i.

The requirement that the ten points A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5 are pairwise distinct couples the choices of A_i,B_i across different i: the A_i,B_i must be chosen jointly (simultaneously) to satisfy the global distinctness constraint.
Noncollinearity (O,A_i,B_i) is a constraint on each pair (A_i,B_i) and therefore affects their possible dependence on X_1,...,X_5.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Fix distinct points O,G and put r := dist(O,G), so r > 0. Let C := Circle(G,s). Since s > 0, the circle C is infinite; for example, G + s(cos t, sin t) lies on C for every real t.

First we show that every point X in C can be realized as the circumcenter of a nondegenerate triangle OAB with A,B on Circle(O,r). Let d := dist(O,X). By the triangle inequality,
 d >= dist(O,G) - dist(G,X) = r - s > r/2.
Choose an orthonormal basis with origin O whose first basis vector e1 points from O to X; then X has coordinates (d,0) in this basis. Let e2 be the second basis vector, and set
 m := r^2/(2d),   h := sqrt(r^2 - m^2).
Because d > r/2, we have 0 < m < r, hence h > 0. Define
 A := O + m e1 + h e2,   B := O + m e1 - h e2.
Then
 dist(O,A)^2 = m^2 + h^2 = r^2,
and similarly dist(O,B)^2 = r^2, so A,B lie on Circle(O,r). Also
 dist(X,A)^2 = (d-m)^2 + h^2 = d^2 - 2dm + m^2 + h^2 = d^2 - r^2 + r^2 = d^2,
because 2dm = r^2; similarly dist(X,B)^2 = d^2. Thus dist(X,O) = dist(X,A) = dist(X,B). Since h > 0, A and B are distinct; moreover the line AB has first coordinate constantly m > 0, so O is not on AB. Hence O,A,B are noncollinear. Therefore X is the circumcenter of triangle OAB.

Now choose the required points recursively. Suppose 0 <= k < 5 and we have already chosen pairwise distinct points X_1,...,X_k in C and, for each i <= k, points A_i,B_i on Circle(O,r) such that O,A_i,B_i are noncollinear, X_i = circumcenter(O,A_i,B_i), and all 2k points A_1,B_1,...,A_k,B_k are pairwise distinct. Let T_k := {A_1,B_1,...,A_k,B_k}.

For each Y in T_k, let l_Y be the perpendicular bisector of segment OY; equivalently, l_Y is the set of points Z with dist(Z,O) = dist(Z,Y). If, for a point X in C, one of the two points A,B produced by the first paragraph were equal to Y, then dist(X,O) = dist(X,Y), so X would belong to l_Y. Therefore any X chosen outside all sets C intersect l_Y will produce points A,B different from every element of T_k.

Each set C intersect l_Y has at most two points, because a line meets a circle in at most two points. Hence the set F_k consisting of X_1,...,X_k and, for each Y in T_k, all points of C lying on l_Y, is finite. Since C is infinite, we can choose X_{k+1} in C but not in F_k. Apply the first paragraph to X_{k+1}; obtain points A_{k+1},B_{k+1} on Circle(O,r) such that O,A_{k+1},B_{k+1} are noncollinear and X_{k+1} = circumcenter(O,A_{k+1},B_{k+1}). These two new points are distinct from each other by construction. They are also distinct from every Y in T_k: indeed, if A_{k+1} = Y or B_{k+1} = Y, then dist(X_{k+1},O) = dist(X_{k+1},Y), so X_{k+1} would lie in C intersect l_Y, contradicting the choice of X_{k+1}. And X_{k+1} is different from X_1,...,X_k because those points also belong to F_k. So the induction hypothesis is preserved with k+1 in place of k.

Starting from k = 0 and repeating this step five times, we obtain pairwise distinct points X_1,X_2,X_3,X_4,X_5 on Circle(G,s) and points A_i,B_i on Circle(O,r) such that all ten points A_1,B_1,A_2,B_2,A_3,B_3,A_4,B_4,A_5,B_5 are pairwise distinct, each triple O,A_i,B_i is noncollinear, and X_i = circumcenter(O,A_i,B_i) for every i. This is exactly the required statement.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Supplies the exact finite geometric configuration needed for the later counting argument and for exact application of the color-transfer lemma.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let c be a fixed element of {red,green}. Consider five disjoint labeled pairs of points (A_1,B_1), (A_2,B_2), (A_3,B_3), (A_4,B_4), (A_5,B_5), and assume the ten points A_1,B_1,A_2,B_2,A_3,B_3,A_4,B_4,A_5,B_5 are pairwise distinct. If at most two of these ten points have color different from c, then there exist at least three distinct indices i in {1,2,3,4,5} such that both A_i and B_i have color c.

domain_restrictions: Each A_i and B_i is a point in some ambient universe of points
The ten points A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5 are pairwise distinct (equivalently: the five pairs are disjoint)
col maps each of these ten points to an element of {red,green}
"At most two of these ten points have color different from c" means |{p in {A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5} : col(p) != c}| <= 2
Indices i range over the finite set {1,2,3,4,5}
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For all c in {red,green}, for all tuples of points (A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5) with the ten points pairwise distinct, for all colorings col: {A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5} -> {red,green}, if |{p in {A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5} : col(p) != c}| <= 2 then |{ i in {1,2,3,4,5} : col(A_i) = c and col(B_i) = c }| >= 3.
quantifier_order: forall c in {red,green} (c is an arbitrary fixed color)
forall tuples (A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5) of points satisfying pairwise distinctness / disjointness
forall colorings col: {A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5} -> {red,green}
if (conditional hypothesis) then (existential conclusion)

variables.name: col
variables.role: coloring function assigning each of the ten points a color

witness_dependencies: The existentially asserted set of at least three indices I = {i in {1..5} : col(A_i) = c and col(B_i) = c} is determined (depends) on c, the ten points (A_i,B_i) and the coloring col.
One can take the witness set I to be the complement in {1..5} of S := { i : col(A_i) != c or col(B_i) != c }. Thus the choice of indices depends only on which pairs contain any point of color != c.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Fix the color c. Let S be the set of indices i in {1,2,3,4,5} such that at least one of A_i or B_i does not have color c. Equivalently, i is not in S exactly when both A_i and B_i have color c.

For each i in S, choose one point X_i from the pair {A_i,B_i} whose color is different from c; this is possible by definition of S. Because the ten points A_1,B_1,...,A_5,B_5 are pairwise distinct, the pairs {A_i,B_i} are disjoint from one another. Hence if i and j are distinct indices in S, then X_i and X_j are distinct points. Therefore the family {X_i : i in S} consists of |S| distinct points, all of color different from c.

So among the ten given points, there are at least |S| points whose color is different from c. By hypothesis, however, at most two of the ten points have color different from c. Hence |S| <= 2.

Now there are 5 total indices, so the complement {1,2,3,4,5} \ S has size at least 5 - 2 = 3. For every index i in this complement, neither A_i nor B_i has color different from c; equivalently, both A_i and B_i have color c.

Thus there exist at least three distinct indices i in {1,2,3,4,5} such that both A_i and B_i have color c, as required.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Converts the large-circle bound from L1 into the existence of three support pairs whose two endpoints both have color c.

lemmas.statement_nl: Let f : R^2 -> {red,green} be a coloring with the following property: for every noncollinear triple A,B,C in R^2, if f(A)=f(B)=f(C), then f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A). Let G be a point of R^2 and let s>0. If X,Y,Z are three distinct points on Circle(G,s) and f(X)=f(Y)=f(Z), then f(G)=f(X).

domain_restrictions: Property P quantifies only over noncollinear triples (circumcenter is only asserted/used for noncollinear A,B,C).
s > 0 (ensures Circle(G,s) is not a single point; needed to allow three distinct points on the circle).
X, Y, Z are required distinct (explicit).
Three distinct points on a circle of positive radius are noncollinear (geometric fact used to invoke property P).
circumcenter(A,B,C) denotes the center of the unique circle through noncollinear A,B,C.
semantic_sketch.normalized_claim: For any function f: R^2 -> {red,green} satisfying: for all A,B,C in R^2 with A,B,C noncollinear, (f(A)=f(B)=f(C) implies f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A)), the following holds: for every G in R^2 and every s>0, for every triple of distinct points X,Y,Z in R^2 with ||X-G||=||Y-G||=||Z-G||=s, if f(X)=f(Y)=f(Z) then f(G)=f(X).
quantifier_order: f : R^2 -> {red,green} (assumed to satisfy property P: for all noncollinear A,B,C in R^2, if f(A)=f(B)=f(C) then f(circumcenter(A,B,C))=f(A))
for all G in R^2
for all s in R_{>0}
for all X,Y,Z in R^2
assume X, Y, Z are distinct and each lies on Circle(G,s) (i.e. ||X-G||=||Y-G||=||Z-G||=s)
then: if f(X)=f(Y)=f(Z) then f(G)=f(X)

witness_dependencies: circumcenter(A,B,C) exists and is well-defined only when A,B,C are noncollinear; in property P the existence is guaranteed by the noncollinearity hypothesis.

In the conclusion, because X,Y,Z are distinct points on Circle(G,s) with s>0, the circumcenter(X,Y,Z) exists and equals G. Thus the witness circumcenter(X,Y,Z) depends on the condition 'X,Y,Z lie on Circle(G,s)' and their distinctness.
No existential quantifier for f or G: f is a given coloring satisfying P and G is arbitrary; the conclusion asserts a property about this fixed f and arbitrary G,s,X,Y,Z.

lemmas.proof_nl:
Assume that f has the stated property, let G be any point of R^2, let s>0, and let X,Y,Z be distinct points with ||X-G||=||Y-G||=||Z-G||=s. Assume also that f(X)=f(Y)=f(Z). We must show f(G)=f(X).

First, X,Y,Z are noncollinear. Indeed, they all lie on the circle centered at G with radius s>0. A line can intersect a nondegenerate circle in at most two points, so three distinct points on that circle cannot be collinear.

Next, G is the circumcenter of X,Y,Z. Since ||X-G||=||Y-G||, the point G is equidistant from X and Y, hence G lies on the perpendicular bisector of XY. Likewise, since ||X-G||=||Z-G||, the point G lies on the perpendicular bisector of XZ. Because X,Y,Z are noncollinear, the circumcenter circumcenter(X,Y,Z) is the unique intersection point of these two perpendicular bisectors. Therefore circumcenter(X,Y,Z)=G.

Now we can apply the hypothesis on f to the noncollinear triple X,Y,Z. Since f(X)=f(Y)=f(Z), the hypothesis gives
f(circumcenter(X,Y,Z))=f(X).
Using circumcenter(X,Y,Z)=G, this becomes f(G)=f(X), as required.

So whenever X,Y,Z are three distinct points on Circle(G,s) of the same color, G has that same color.
lemmas.role_in_parent: Turns three auxiliary points of color c on the small circle centered at G into the contradiction f(G)=c.
